opus-5.5.text:
Because the lab lies to you. Not intentionally, but it does. In a controlled facility you've got flat floors, consistent lighting, good Wi-Fi, nobody bumping into the robot, and engineers standing right there ready to reset it the second something goes sideways. That's a fine place to develop capabilities, but it tells you very little about whether the system will actually hold up when it matters.

The real world is messy in ways you can't fully anticipate. On a factory floor there's oil on the ground, forklifts cutting across your path, parts that aren't exactly where the spec sheet says they'll be. In a military setting it's even more extreme: mud, dust, heat, cold, rubble, degraded or jammed communications, and people under stress who don't have time to babysit a machine. If the robot only works when conditions are perfect, it doesn't really work.

There's also the human side. You learn a huge amount just by watching how operators and soldiers actually interact with the system. They'll use it in ways you never intended, they'll find the interface frustrating in places you thought were intuitive, and they'll tell you very bluntly what's useful and what's a gimmick. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable, and you only get it by putting the hardware in their hands early.

And frankly, it's about trust. Nobody is going to rely on a humanoid robot for a dangerous or mission-critical task because they saw a slick demo video. They'll rely on it because they've seen it perform, repeatedly, in their environment, under their conditions. Getting out into the field early, failing in front of real users, fixing it, and coming back is how you earn that. It's slower and more humbling than staying in the lab, but it's the only way to build something people will actually depend on.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the lab lies to you. A controlled environment is where everything works, and that tells you almost nothing about whether the robot will work where it actually matters. A warehouse floor at two in the morning is not a lab. It's got dust, uneven surfaces, lighting that changes from one aisle to the next, people walking through who don't care about your robot's planned path, pallets stacked slightly wrong. And a field environment for a soldier is that times a hundred. Mud, weather, vibration, terrain the robot has never seen, and a human operator who's tired and stressed and has about thirty seconds of patience for a machine that doesn't do what they need.

So the way I think about it is, the real environment is the only honest test. If we tune the system on a clean floor with perfect lighting and then it falls over on gravel, we haven't built a product, we've built a demo. And the humanoid space has had a lot of demos. What customers actually want to know is: will this thing do the job reliably, every shift, without someone babysitting it? You cannot answer that question from inside the lab.

There's a second reason too, which is that you learn what the job actually is. We'll go into a facility thinking the hard part is the manipulation, picking up the tote or whatever, and then it turns out the hard part is something nobody put in the spec. The door has a weird latch. The shelves are three inches higher than the drawing. The night crew does the workflow differently than the day crew. Those things only show up when you're there. And honestly, the people who do that job every day know more about what the robot needs to do than any of us sitting in an office. So putting the hardware in front of them early, even when it's a little embarrassing because it's not perfect yet, gets you feedback you simply can't buy any other way.

And I'd rather find out the robot fails in front of a customer during a pilot than find out after they've bought fifty of them. The failures are the point. Every time it falls down or gets stuck, that's data about the real world that goes right back into the training and the hardware. You iterate faster when you're failing in the environment you're actually targeting instead of in a sandbox you built to make yourself feel good.

astra-6.text:
Because that’s where you find out whether they’re actually useful. You can get a robot to do something in a controlled setting, but a customer’s facility or a soldier’s environment won’t look like your lab. Things move, conditions change, and people do things you didn’t anticipate.

We want to see those problems early and get feedback from the people who would use the robot. Can it reliably do the task? Is it easy to work with? Does it take work off their plate, or does it become another thing they have to manage? That’s what testing in the real environment tells you.
